jlbind lets R packages call Julia code compiled ahead of time into a shared
library, without a Julia session. This vignette explains how that library works
and how to use an R package built with jlbind. To add Julia functions to your
own R package, see [Get started with jlbind](jlbind.html). For how jlbind
compares with other ways of calling Julia from R, see
[Performance](https://bjarkehautop.github.io/jlbind/vignettes/articles/performance.html).

## How it works

An R process can load only one compiled Julia library. Julia has one runtime per
process, and that runtime uses a single compiled image. If two R packages loaded
separate copies of the library, they could conflict and crash the R session.

To avoid this, jlbind builds one shared library for each user, combining the
Julia code of all installed R packages that use jlbind (*clients*). When you run
`install_library()`, jlbind finds the installed clients, compiles their binding
packages into one library, and saves it under
`tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "data")`. Loading a client loads that library and
connects the client to it.

A client can only be bound to a library built from the version of that client
currently installed. If you update a package without rebuilding the library, its
functions will report that the library needs to be rebuilt.

## Using a package built on jlbind

You need [Julia](https://julialang.org/install/) 1.13 or later to build the
shared library.

After installing or updating an R package that uses jlbind, run:

```r
jlbind::install_library()
```

The first build downloads and compiles the required Julia dependencies, so it
may take a few minutes.

::: {.callout-note}
**Restart R after rebuilding a library that is already loaded**

Julia cannot be restarted within an R session. If the old library has already
been loaded, rebuilding it on disk does not replace the copy in memory. Restart
R to use the new library.
:::

### If something doesn't work correctly

If a package that uses jlbind doesn't work, first check its status:

```r
jlbind::check_bound("somepkg")
```

The most common causes are that the shared library hasn't been built yet, or
that the package was updated after the last build. For a full report, run:

```r
jlbind::jlbind_sitrep()
```

It shows the Julia that `install_library()` would use (with its version, and
whether it came from `JULIA` or the `PATH`), the library and what it was built
from, each installed package that uses jlbind and whether the library is current
for it, and the thread count. It works whether or not a library has loaded, and
returns the same information invisibly as a list.

If the Julia installation used for the build has been removed or replaced, for
example by a `juliaup` update, rebuild the library. `install_library()` rebuilds
it when the Julia version differs from the one it was built with. If the version
is the same, use `force = TRUE`:

```r
jlbind::install_library(force = TRUE)
```

You can select the Julia installation to use by setting the `JULIA` environment
variable or by passing `julia =` to `install_library()`.

The library is compiled for the building machine's CPU. To use it on other
machines (e.g. cluster nodes), set `JULIA_CPU_TARGET=generic` and rebuild with
`force = TRUE`.

### Threads

Julia runs with one thread by default. To use multiple threads, set
`JULIA_NUM_THREADS` before loading the first package that uses jlbind, for
example in your `.Renviron` file:

```sh
JULIA_NUM_THREADS=auto # or a number, such as 4
```

The thread count is fixed when the library is loaded, so restart R after
changing it.

### Dependency versions

All clients share a single set of Julia dependencies. By default, the build
starts from the versions in the `Manifest.toml` of the first client that has
one, and keeps them for the other clients where their `[compat]` bounds allow.
Pass `versions = "compat"` to ignore the manifests and let Julia's resolver
choose versions from the clients' `[compat]` bounds alone.

If a client's `[compat]` bounds conflict with those of the clients listed before
it by `jlbind_clients()`, it is left out of the build; `check_bound()` says
which clients it conflicts with.

You can control which clients are included by specifying them explicitly:

```r
jlbind::install_library(packages = c("pkgA", "pkgC"))
```

::: {.callout-important}
**Clients with incompatible dependencies cannot share a library**

If you need both clients but never need them in the same R session, build a
separate library for each. Set `JLBIND_LIBRARY` before loading the client to
select the library for that session.

For example, build the two libraries:

```r
jlbind::build_library("pkgA", "~/jlbind/pkgA")
jlbind::build_library("pkgB", "~/jlbind/pkgB")
```

Then select one in an R session:

```r
# jlbind.dll on Windows, jlbind.dylib on macOS
Sys.setenv(JLBIND_LIBRARY = "~/jlbind/pkgA/jlbind.so")
library(pkgA)
```
:::
